title: Truncation triangles in the unbounded finite-filtered localization
statement: Let $\mathcal C$ be an abelian category [def-sp-abelian], and let $DF(\mathcal C)$ be the localization of all cochain complexes with a uniformly finite decreasing filtration by subcomplexes [def-sp-filtration, def-sp-filtered-complex-subquotients] at maps that are quasi-isomorphisms on every graded complex, with localizations in a common larger universe. The localization has the triangulated structure [def-weil-triangulated-category] induced by filtered mapping cones. Forgetting the filtration $\omega:DF(\mathcal C)\to D(\mathcal C)$ [def-weil-abstract-derived-category] and each graded-piece functor $\operatorname{gr}^p:DF(\mathcal C)\to D(\mathcal C)$ are exact. An object is supported in an interval when its graded objects outside that interval vanish in $D(\mathcal C)$. For every integer $r$, the subcomplex and quotient constructions $t_{\ge r}M=F^rM$ and $t_{<r}M=M/F^rM$ descend to exact functors on $DF(\mathcal C)$; their graded pieces are respectively $\operatorname{gr}^pM$ for $p\ge r$ and $p<r$, and zero otherwise. They form a natural distinguished triangle $t_{\ge r}M\to M\to t_{<r}M\to(t_{\ge r}M)[1]$. This triangle is unique up to the unique isomorphism inducing the identity on $M$ among distinguished triangles whose first term has grades only in indices $\ge r$ and whose third term has grades only in indices $<r$. For $L$ supported in grades $\ge r$ and $R$ supported in grades $<r$, composition with the canonical inclusion and quotient gives natural bijections $\operatorname{Hom}(L,t_{\ge r}M)\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Hom}(L,M)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}(t_{<r}M,R)\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Hom}(M,R)$. Thus $t_{\ge r}$ is right adjoint to the inclusion of the first support subcategory, and $t_{<r}$ is left adjoint to the inclusion of the second. Consequently $T_p=t_{\ge p}t_{<p+1}$ has only grade $p$, and $\omega T_p=\operatorname{gr}^p$ naturally; on objects with only grade $p$, $T_p$ is the identity and forgetting the filtration is an equivalence with the ordinary derived category.

source.place: §5.1.1(a)–(d), §5.1.2(a)–(c), pp.39–40; the adjoint directions printed in §5.1.1(c) are reversed (see Source error in report.md).

proof.text: Let $\mathcal B$ be the category of finite decreasingly filtered objects of $\mathcal C$. Filtered maps are closed under addition, and the zero object and binary direct sums with $F^p(X\oplus Y)=F^pX\oplus F^pY$ give zero and biproducts. Thus [lem-trf-additive-homotopy-category-triangulated] applies to $K(\mathcal B)$. Let $\mathcal K$ be its full subcategory of complexes with a uniform finite filtration interval. Shifts retain the interval, and a cone on objects with bounds $[a,b]$ and $[c,d]$ has bounds $[\min(a,c),\max(b,d)]$. Let $K\to L\to M\to K[1]$ be distinguished with $K,M\in\mathcal K$. By (TR2) of [def-weil-triangulated-category] its backward rotation $M[-1]\xrightarrow{u}K\to L\to M$ is distinguished. Choose a chain map $f:M[-1]\to K$ representing $u$; the cone triangle of $f$ is distinguished with the same first two terms and first map, so (TR3) gives a morphism of triangles $(1,1,c)$ from it to the rotated triangle, and $c:C(f)\to L$ is an isomorphism by [lem-sf-triangle-morphism-iso]. Hence $L\cong C(f)\in\mathcal K$. Therefore $\mathcal K$ is triangulated with this cone structure by [def-weil-triangulated-subcategory]. There is no bound on cochain degrees.

source.place: Tags 05RX (section-filtered-derived-category), 014S (proposition-homotopy-category-triangulated), 05QM (definition-triangulated-subcategory); restrict to uniformly finite filtrations

proof.text: The localization in the statement also localizes $\mathcal K$. Indeed, for filtered chain maps with $f-g=dh+hd$, use $\operatorname{Cyl}(X)^n=X^n\oplus X^{n+1}\oplus X^n$ with differential $(a,b,c)\mapsto(da-b,-db,dc+b)$ and direct-sum filtration. The outer inclusions $i_0,i_1$ and $p(a,b,c)=a+c$ satisfy $pi_0=pi_1=1$. The filtered homotopy $H(a,b,c)=(0,c,0)$ satisfies $dH+Hd=1-i_0p$, so $p$ is a homotopy equivalence on every grade and belongs to $W$. The chain map $\varphi(a,b,c)=f(a)-h(b)+g(c)$ satisfies $\varphi i_0=f$, $\varphi i_1=g$. Inverting $p$ identifies the two inclusions, hence $f$ and $g$. The cylinder has the same uniform bounds as $X$. Consequently every functor inverting $W$ factors through filtered homotopies; the universal property [lem-weil-pbc-localization-universal-property] identifies the chain-complex localization with $\mathcal K[W^{-1}]$, including natural transformations.

source.place: §5.1.2(a); explicit filtered cylinder for the passage from complexes to homotopy classes

proof.text: Grading commutes with shifts and cones: $\operatorname{gr}^pC(f)=C(\operatorname{gr}^pf)$, since the filtration on a cone is the direct-sum filtration and quotienting a finite direct sum gives the direct sum of the quotients. The cone criterion [lem-pur-quasi-iso-cone-acyclic] therefore identifies $W$ with the maps having graded-acyclic cone. Any distinguished triangle $X\xrightarrow{u}Y\to Z\to X[1]$ of $\mathcal K$ has $Z\cong C(u)$: (TR3) of [def-weil-triangulated-category] gives a morphism $(1,1,c)$ from the cone triangle of a representative of $u$, and $c$ is an isomorphism by [lem-sf-triangle-morphism-iso]. Since graded acyclicity is invariant under isomorphism in $\mathcal K$, $W$ is exactly the class of maps having some distinguished triangle with third vertex graded acyclic. Let $\mathcal P$ be the full replete subcategory of graded-acyclic objects of $\mathcal K$. It contains zero and is closed under all shifts. A cone on a map between two objects of $\mathcal P$ is in $\mathcal P$: on every grade this is a map of acyclic complexes, hence a quasi-isomorphism, whose cone is acyclic by the same criterion. For a distinguished triangle with two vertices in $\mathcal P$, rotate them into the first two places; by the isomorphism $Z\cong C(u)$ just proved the third vertex is a cone of a map in $\mathcal P$, hence in $\mathcal P$. Thus $\mathcal P$ is triangulated. Apply [lem-trf-triangulated-subcategory-cone-system] to get both calculi of fractions and compatibility with triangles; apply [lem-pur-localization-triangles-05r6] to triangulate $DF(\mathcal C)$ with $Q$ exact and distinguished triangles precisely the images of cone triangles up to isomorphism.

Define $A_rK=F^rK$ and $B_rK=K/F^rK$. Induced and quotient filtrations give $F^p(A_rK)=F^{\max(p,r)}K$ and $F^p(B_rK)=F^{\min(p,r)}K/F^rK$. Taking successive quotients therefore gives $\operatorname{gr}^p(A_rK)=\operatorname{gr}^pK$ for $p\ge r$ and zero for $p<r$, while $\operatorname{gr}^p(B_rK)=\operatorname{gr}^pK$ for $p<r$ and zero for $p\ge r$. These are natural identifications from the subquotient definitions. The bounds remain finite, including when a truncation is zero. Filtered maps and homotopies restrict to $F^r$ and descend to the quotient, giving additive functors on $\mathcal K$. Their graded formulas show that they preserve $W$. They thus descend by [lem-weil-pbc-localization-universal-property]. On cones one has $A_rC(f)=C(A_rf)$ and $B_rC(f)=C(B_rf)$, with the same inclusion and projection maps and shift signs. By the image-of-cones description in Step 3 both descended functors are exact. They are the asserted $t_{\ge r},t_{<r}$.

source.place: §5.1.1(b)–(d), §5.1.2(b): induced and quotient filtrations and their descent

proof.text: A graded-acyclic uniformly filtered complex $Z$ is acyclic after forgetting the filtration. Choose $F^aZ=Z$, $F^{b+1}Z=0$. For each $p=b,b-1,\ldots,a$, the degreewise short exact sequence $0\to F^{p+1}Z\to F^pZ\to\operatorname{gr}^pZ\to0$ and [lem-weil-pbc-complex-ses-homology-long-exact] show that $F^pZ$ is acyclic if $F^{p+1}Z$ is: in the long exact sequence the groups on either side of $H^n(F^pZ)$ vanish for every $n$. The induction starts at the zero complex. For $s\in W$, Step 3 says $C(s)$ is graded acyclic; the induction makes its underlying cone acyclic. Hence the underlying $s$ is a quasi-isomorphism by [lem-pur-quasi-iso-cone-acyclic]. Forgetting thus descends by [lem-weil-pbc-localization-universal-property]; grading descends by the definition of $W$. Both commute with shifts, cone matrices, and cone arrows, so both are exact by Step 3. Uniform finiteness, rather than any cochain boundedness, is what makes the induction finite.

source.place: Tag 05S3 (lemma-filtered-derived-functors); finite filtration induction using the long exact cohomology sequence

proof.text: For $i:A_rM\hookrightarrow M$, the cone formula gives a natural filtered chain map $c:C(i)\to B_rM$ by $(m,a)\mapsto\overline m$. Its grade for $p<r$ is the identity from $C(0\to\operatorname{gr}^pM)$ to $\operatorname{gr}^pM$; for $p\ge r$ its source is $C(1_{\operatorname{gr}^pM})$ and its target is zero. The latter cone is contractible: with differential $(y,x)\mapsto(dy+x,-dx)$ the homotopy $(y,x)\mapsto(0,y)$ contracts the identity. Thus $c\in W$. Replace $QC(i)$ in its distinguished cone triangle by $QB_rM$ using $Q(c)$. The first two arrows become inclusion and quotient and the last becomes $\delta_M=-Q(p)Q(c)^{-1}$ with $p:C(i)\to(A_rM)[1]$. This proves the triangle in the statement with its specified connecting map. For a filtered chain map, the diagonal map of cones commutes with $c$, the inclusions, and $p$; therefore it commutes with $\delta$. These identities descend to the localization by [lem-weil-pbc-localization-universal-property], giving naturality also for localized morphisms.

source.place: §5.1.2(c), constructing the truncation triangle by its cone and quotient comparison

proof.text: If $L$ is supported in grades $\ge r$, the map $A_rL\to L$ induces the identity on those grades and $0\to\operatorname{gr}^pL$ on the remaining, acyclic grades; it is a graded quasi-isomorphism. Similarly $R\to B_rR$ is a graded quasi-isomorphism for $R$ supported in grades $<r$. Thus each high-supported object has a representative with $F^rL=L$ literally, and each low-supported object has one with $F^rR=0$ literally. This uses only the graded formulas of Step 4 and the definition of a quasi-isomorphism, and works with acyclic, nonzero graded complexes. All cochain shifts of these representatives have the same filtration support.

source.place: §5.1.2(a)–(b), representing derived filtration support by strict filtration bounds

proof.text: We now show $\operatorname{Hom}(L,R[q])=0$ for every integer $q$ when $L$ is high-supported and $R$ low-supported. Use the strict representatives of Step 7. By Step 3 and [lem-pc-right-fraction-representation], a morphism is $Q(f)Q(s)^{-1}$ for $s:Z\to L$ in $W$ and $f:Z\to R[q]$ in $\mathcal K$. The map $a:A_rZ\to Z$ belongs to $W$: for $p\ge r$ its graded map is the identity; for $p<r$, $\operatorname{gr}^pZ$ is acyclic because $s$ identifies its cohomology with that of $\operatorname{gr}^pL=0$, so $0\to\operatorname{gr}^pZ$ is a quasi-isomorphism. Now $fa=0$ since a filtered map sends its source $F^rZ$ into $F^r(R[q])=0$. In the localization $Q(f)Q(s)^{-1}=Q(fa)Q(sa)^{-1}=0$. The finite filtration bounds of $A_rZ$ are retained by Step 4. No assertion about fullness of a bounded-cochain subcategory is needed.

source.place: §5.1.2(a)–(c); explicit right-roof proof of the semiorthogonality behind the truncation adjunctions

proof.text: For $g:L\to M$ with $L$ high-supported, compare the distinguished triangle $L\xrightarrow1L\to0\to L[1]$ with the canonical triangle $A_rM\to M\to B_rM\to(A_rM)[1]$, taking $g$ as middle map. Their relevant composite is zero by Step 8. Part (1) of [lem-weil-pbc-triangle-morphism-extension] gives $f:L\to A_rM$ with $i_Mf=g$; part (2) gives uniqueness because $\operatorname{Hom}(L[1],B_rM)=0$ by Step 8. Thus composition with $i_M$ is bijective. For $g:M\to R$ with $R$ low-supported, compare the canonical triangle with $0\to R\xrightarrow1R\to0$, which is distinguished by rotation of the identity triangle. Step 8 makes $gi_M=0$ and $\operatorname{Hom}((A_rM)[1],R)=0$. The same parts of the lemma give a unique $h:B_rM\to R$ with $hq_M=g$. These composition bijections are natural in $L$ and $R$ by associativity and in $M$ by the naturality proved in Step 6. They give precisely the right adjoint $t_{\ge r}$ and the left adjoint $t_{<r}$ to the respective inclusions.

source.place: §5.1.1(c) (adjoint directions corrected), §5.1.2(b); adjunction from the canonical triangle and orthogonality

proof.text: Consider any distinguished $L\to M\to R\to L[1]$ with $L$ high-supported and $R$ low-supported. Step 8 makes the composite $L\to M\to B_rM$ zero, so [lem-weil-pbc-triangle-morphism-extension](1) supplies a map to the canonical truncation triangle whose middle map is $1_M$. Its first and third components are unique by part (2), since $\operatorname{Hom}(L[1],B_rM)=0$. Interchanging the two triangles similarly gives a map back, unique because $\operatorname{Hom}((A_rM)[1],R)=0$. Both composites are the identity morphisms of triangles by uniqueness for middle map $1_M$ (including uniqueness on each triangle itself). Hence the comparison is a unique isomorphism inducing $1_M$. This also checks the connecting square rather than merely the first two squares.

source.place: §5.1.2(c), uniqueness of the distinguished truncation triangle

proof.text: Set $T_p=A_pB_{p+1}$. By Step 4 its only surviving grade is $p$, and the subquotient formulas identify its underlying complex with $F^pM/F^{p+1}M=\operatorname{gr}^pM$. These formulas are natural for filtered maps; localization of their natural isomorphism gives $\omega T_p\cong\operatorname{gr}^p$ by [lem-weil-pbc-localization-universal-property]. On complexes $T_pM$ has its entire underlying complex in filtration degrees $\le p$ and zero in degrees $>p$. Define $J_p$ on ordinary complexes by this pure filtration. It sends quasi-isomorphisms to graded quasi-isomorphisms, so descends to $J_p:D(\mathcal C)\to DF(\mathcal C)$ by the same localization property, with $\omega J_p=1$ and $J_p\operatorname{gr}^p\cong T_p$. Its compatibility with cone formulas also makes it exact.

source.place: §5.1.1(b),(d), §5.1.2(b): pure filtration and the graded-piece formula

proof.text: Restrict to objects supported in the single grade $p$. There is a natural zigzag $M\longrightarrow B_{p+1}M\longleftarrow A_pB_{p+1}M=T_pM$. Each arrow is a graded quasi-isomorphism: it is the identity on grade $p$ and compares acyclic complexes with zero on all removed grades. It follows that $T_p\cong1$ on this full subcategory. Applying $\omega$ to this zigzag identifies $\omega M$ naturally with $\omega T_pM\cong\operatorname{gr}^pM$, while Step 11 identifies $J_p\operatorname{gr}^pM$ with $T_pM$. Thus $J_p\omega\cong1$ on the pure subcategory; together with $\omega J_p=1$ this gives the asserted equivalence with the entire ordinary unbounded derived category. Inverting the first arrow and then the second as needed specifies the isomorphisms, so no nonexistent direct map $T_pM\to M$ is presumed.

source.place: §5.1.1(d), §5.1.2(a)–(b): the pure-grade equivalence, with acyclic exterior grades
